Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

Every category has a bidirectional nature. For example:

One person's sensitivity to the Care/Harm foundation may lead them to support high levels of immigration from poorer nations, to reduce the suffering of those who migrate. Whereas another person's sensitivity to the very same foundation may lead them to oppose those levels, because they believe it could lead to people they care about being harmed.

# Summary of the 2015 Manifesto

## Economic Policy
The document outlines a plan to eliminate the budget deficit through continued spending reductions, targeting £30 billion in savings over two years through departmental cuts, welfare savings, and tackling tax avoidance. The goal is achieving a budget surplus by 2018-19. Commitments include no increases to VAT, National Insurance, or Income Tax rates, while raising the tax-free Personal Allowance to £12,500 and the higher rate threshold to £50,000.

## Regional Development
Plans include creating a "Northern Powerhouse" through £13 billion in northern transport investment, rail electrification, and High Speed 2/3 development. Similar investment commitments cover the Midlands, South West, and East of England, with devolution of powers to cities choosing elected mayors.

## Infrastructure
The manifesto commits over £100 billion to infrastructure, including £38 billion for railways, £15 billion for roads, and universal broadband coverage. Promises include freezing commuter rail fares in real terms and improving mobile coverage to 90% of UK landmass.

## Employment and Business
The plan targets full employment through creating two million jobs and three million apprenticeships. Business support includes maintaining competitive corporation tax, reviewing business rates, cutting £10 billion in regulation, and expanding export support.

## Welfare Reform
Proposals include capping household benefits at £23,000 annually, continuing Universal Credit rollout, freezing working-age benefits for two years, and introducing stricter requirements for young jobseekers including a time-limited Youth Allowance.

## Immigration
The document proposes requiring EU migrants to live in the UK for four years before claiming tax credits or social housing, ending child benefit payments for children living abroad, and strengthening border controls and deportation powers.

## Education
Commitments include protecting per-pupil funding, converting failing schools to academies, opening 500 free schools, training additional maths and physics teachers, and removing caps on university places.

## Healthcare
The NHS would receive £8 billion additional funding by 2020, with goals including seven-day GP and hospital access, same-day appointments for over-75s, and improved mental health services. Integration of health and social care continues through the Better Care Fund.

## Housing
Housing policies include building 200,000 Starter Homes at 20% below market price for first-time buyers under 40, extending Right to Buy to housing association tenants, continuing Help to Buy schemes, and introducing Help to Buy ISAs.

## Energy and Environment
The plan supports nuclear power, shale gas development, and ending subsidies for onshore wind farms. Environmental commitments include marine protection zones, flood defence investment, and meeting climate change targets cost-effectively.

## Pensions and Elderly Care
The triple lock on state pensions continues, alongside introducing a single-tier pension, maintaining pension freedoms, and capping residential care costs. Inheritance tax changes would effectively raise the threshold for married couples to £1 million.

## Constitutional Matters
Proposals include holding an EU referendum by end of 2017, implementing "English votes for English laws," honouring devolution commitments to Scotland and Wales, and replacing the Human Rights Act with a domestic Bill of Rights.

## Defence and Foreign Policy
Commitments include maintaining armed forces at current levels, building four successor nuclear submarines, meeting NATO's 2% GDP defence spending target, and maintaining the 0.7% overseas aid commitment while focusing on specific outcomes including child immunisation and disease eradication.

# Summary of 2015 UK General Election Manifesto

## Economic Policy

The manifesto commits to cutting the deficit annually and achieving a budget surplus, with all policies fully funded without additional borrowing. Proposals include maintaining competitive corporate tax rates, cutting and freezing business rates for small businesses, abolishing non-domicile tax status, and closing tax loopholes. A new British Investment Bank would support small and medium businesses, with regional banks expanding access to finance.

## Employment and Wages

Key proposals include raising the minimum wage to over £8 per hour by 2019, banning exploitative zero-hours contracts, and promoting the Living Wage through government procurement. A jobs guarantee would provide paid work for long-term unemployed young people and adults.

## Education and Skills

The manifesto pledges to protect the entire education budget, reduce university tuition fees to £6,000, guarantee apprenticeships for qualified school leavers, and cap primary school class sizes. All state school teachers would require qualified teacher status, with new Directors of School Standards providing local oversight.

## Healthcare and Social Care

Proposals include recruiting 8,000 additional GPs, 20,000 nurses, and 3,000 midwives, funded through a property tax on high-value homes and tobacco levies. The manifesto promises 48-hour GP appointment guarantees, integrated physical, mental and social care services, and recruitment of 5,000 home-care workers.

## Housing

Targets include building 200,000 homes annually by 2020, introducing three-year tenancies with rent rise limits, banning unfair letting fees, creating a landlord register, and abolishing the spare room subsidy affecting benefit recipients.

## Immigration and Borders

Proposals include hiring 1,000 additional border staff, implementing exit checks, requiring two-year residency before benefit claims, and mandating English language skills for public-facing workers.

## Constitutional Reform

The manifesto proposes extending voting rights to 16-17 year olds, replacing the upper parliamentary chamber with an elected regional senate, significant devolution of powers and £30 billion funding to English regions, and implementing agreed devolution settlements for Scotland and Wales.

## Foreign Policy and Defence

Commitments include maintaining membership of major international alliances, conducting a defence review, maintaining nuclear deterrent capability, and committing 0.7% of national income to international development. Climate change action features prominently, with targets for net-zero emissions and ambitious international climate agreements.
